title: The A / B / C Move Ladder

story.text: How do we classify interventions against complexity rent so that we can apply the minimum effective force and avoid triggering immune responses?

The A/B/C move ladder classifies interventions by the institutional power required and the risk incurred. A-moves change conversations, B-moves change local procedures, and C-moves change incentive structures. Using the wrong level of intervention is ineffective or dangerous; using the right level is efficient and safe.
Interventions that operate entirely inside existing conversations, without changing rules, roles, or authority structures.
None beyond being a legitimate participant.
Redirect discourse away from status, identity, and virtue, and toward cost, constraints, lifecycle, and legibility.

* “What concrete metric defines ‘scale’ here?”
* “What is the lifecycle cost curve of this choice?”
* “How long should it take a competent outsider to understand this?”
* “What would we delete if we add this?”
A-moves fail when incentives contradict answers. The conversation acknowledges the question but proceeds unchanged.
Interventions that modify local procedures: how decisions are recorded, evaluated, or enforced within a bounded scope (team, service, project).
Process, checklists, review criteria, ownership structure.
Local mandate (tech lead, team lead, senior engineer).
Medium. Can trigger resistance but is defensible as “process improvement.”
Make previously rhetorical values (simplicity, legibility, cost) operational and enforceable.

* Adding lifecycle accounting to ADRs
* Establishing complexity budgets
* Making deletion and simplification promotion-visible
* Rotating ownership to expose hidden rents
B-moves fail when org-level incentives quietly override them (they exist on paper, not in practice).
Interventions that alter what the organization rewards, promotes, and legitimizes.
Promotion criteria, performance reviews, career ladders, executive signaling.
High. Politically charged. Hard to reverse.
Eliminate the root cause by aligning career rationality with system health.

* Redefining seniority as entropy reduction
* Rewarding simplification explicitly in promotion packets
* Attaching maintenance accountability to complexity introduction
* Publicly celebrating decommissioning
Attempted without mandate, C-moves trigger immune responses: “political,” “negative,” “not how we do things.”
The ladder encodes minimum effective intervention.

* If an A-move works, escalating is wasteful and risky.
* If A-moves fail repeatedly, staying at A-level is naïve.
* If B-moves are bypassed, the problem is not persuasion—it is incentives.
* If you lack C-move authority, attempting them directly is self-sabotage.

A-moves change conversations.
B-moves change behavior.
C-moves change systems.
The ladder aligns with epistemic defense patterns.

* Standing claims / criterion elevation → countered by A-moves
* Jurisdictional pullbacks → countered by B-moves
* Closure mechanisms → removable only by C-moves

1. Start with A-moves.
2. Escalate to B-moves when patterns repeat.
3. Use C-moves only with mandate—or treat their absence as diagnostic information about the organization itself.

* Attempting C-moves without authority.
* Staying at A-level when B-moves are necessary.
* Using B-moves without team buy-in.

* “We just need to have the right conversation.” (when incentives are misaligned)
* “Process will fix this.” (when process is undermined by promotion criteria)
* “We need to change the culture.” (without changing incentives)

The ladder is not about moral quality, but operational scope and risk.
Moves from different levels may be combined if authority permits, but the risk profile changes accordingly.

* Use this page to plan interventions against complexity rent.
* When facing resistance, diagnose whether the current move level is appropriate.
* Share with allies to coordinate escalation without overstepping.

item.title: The A / B / C Move Ladder

item.text: Intervention Scope and Risk
Tags: #software_engineering #governance #intervention #complexity #epistemic_governance #protocol

question
How do we classify interventions against complexity rent so that we can apply the minimum effective force and avoid triggering immune responses?

claim
The A/B/C move ladder classifies interventions by the institutional power required and the risk incurred. A-moves change conversations, B-moves change local procedures, and C-moves change incentive structures. Using the wrong level of intervention is ineffective or dangerous; using the right level is efficient and safe.

support

A-moves — Conversational / Framing Interventions

What they are
Interventions that operate entirely inside existing conversations, without changing rules, roles, or authority structures.

What they act on
Framing, criteria, vocabulary, attention.

Authority required
None beyond being a legitimate participant.

Risk profile
Low. Social friction at most.

Purpose
Redirect discourse away from status, identity, and virtue, and toward cost, constraints, lifecycle, and legibility.

Canonical examples

* “What concrete metric defines ‘scale’ here?”
* “What is the lifecycle cost curve of this choice?”
* “How long should it take a competent outsider to understand this?”
* “What would we delete if we add this?”

Failure mode
A-moves fail when incentives contradict answers. The conversation acknowledges the question but proceeds unchanged.

---

B-moves — Procedural / Team-Level Governance Interventions

What they are
Interventions that modify local procedures: how decisions are recorded, evaluated, or enforced within a bounded scope (team, service, project).

What they act on
Process, checklists, review criteria, ownership structure.

Authority required
Local mandate (tech lead, team lead, senior engineer).

Risk profile
Medium. Can trigger resistance but is defensible as “process improvement.”

Purpose
Make previously rhetorical values (simplicity, legibility, cost) operational and enforceable.

Canonical examples

* Adding lifecycle accounting to ADRs
* Establishing complexity budgets
* Making deletion and simplification promotion-visible
* Rotating ownership to expose hidden rents

Failure mode
B-moves fail when org-level incentives quietly override them (they exist on paper, not in practice).

---

C-moves — Institutional / Incentive-Level Interventions

What they are
Interventions that alter what the organization rewards, promotes, and legitimizes.

What they act on
Promotion criteria, performance reviews, career ladders, executive signaling.

Authority required
High (management, leadership, org design).

Risk profile
High. Politically charged. Hard to reverse.

Purpose
Eliminate the root cause by aligning career rationality with system health.

Canonical examples

* Redefining seniority as entropy reduction
* Rewarding simplification explicitly in promotion packets
* Attaching maintenance accountability to complexity introduction
* Publicly celebrating decommissioning

Failure mode
Attempted without mandate, C-moves trigger immune responses: “political,” “negative,” “not how we do things.”

---

Why the distinction matters

The ladder encodes minimum effective intervention.

* If an A-move works, escalating is wasteful and risky.
* If A-moves fail repeatedly, staying at A-level is naïve.
* If B-moves are bypassed, the problem is not persuasion—it is incentives.
* If you lack C-move authority, attempting them directly is self-sabotage.

In short:
A-moves change conversations.
B-moves change behavior.
C-moves change systems.

---

Epistemic mapping

The ladder aligns with epistemic defense patterns.

* Standing claims / criterion elevation → countered by A-moves
* Jurisdictional pullbacks → countered by B-moves
* Closure mechanisms → removable only by C-moves

---

Practical rule of thumb

1. Start with A-moves.
2. Escalate to B-moves when patterns repeat.
3. Use C-moves only with mandate—or treat their absence as diagnostic information about the organization itself.

tripwires

* Attempting C-moves without authority.
* Staying at A-level when B-moves are necessary.
* Using B-moves without team buy-in.

rationalizations

* “We just need to have the right conversation.” (when incentives are misaligned)
* “Process will fix this.” (when process is undermined by promotion criteria)
* “We need to change the culture.” (without changing incentives)

oppose
The ladder is not about moral quality, but operational scope and risk.
Moves from different levels may be combined if authority permits, but the risk profile changes accordingly.

* Use this page to plan interventions against complexity rent.
* When facing resistance, diagnose whether the current move level is appropriate.
* Share with allies to coordinate escalation without overstepping.
